title: Roundtables: A Conversation with the Creator of AI-Designed Viruses
content:
Roundtables: A Conversation With the Creator of AI-Designed Viruses
Join a subscriber-only conversation with one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35.
Available only for MIT Technology Review subscribers.
Friday, October 16, 2026
Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. Join senior AI reporter James O'Donnell as he interviews King about his work, being named one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 and new ways of seeing biology.
Going live on October 16th at 18:30 BST / 1:30pm EDT / 10:30am PDT
Speakers: James O'Donnell, AI Reporter, and Samuel King, Bioengineering PhD Candidate, Stanford University/Arc Institute

report.summary: MIT Technology Review will host a roundtable with Samuel King, who used generative AI to propose genetic blueprints for viruses.
report.background: Generative AI is moving from text and images into biology, where models can suggest protein structures, genetic sequences, and even viral designs. In 2025, Stanford PhD student Samuel King used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It is not yet AI-generated life, but it points toward a future where AI could help design biological systems. The work sits at the intersection of synthetic biology, genome design, and biosecurity. MIT Technology Review's subscriber-only Roundtables event on October 16, 2026, will feature King in conversation with senior AI reporter James O'Donnell, exploring his Innovators Under 35 recognition and what new AI-driven views of biology may mean.
key_points: The event is a subscriber-only MIT Technology Review Roundtable on October 16, 2026, featuring senior AI reporter James O'Donnell interviewing Samuel King, a Stanford bioengineering PhD candidate and Arc Institute researcher named to Innovators Under 35.

In 2025, King used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. The article stresses this is not yet AI-generated life, but a preliminary step that could lead to it next.
The conversation will explore new ways of seeing biology, likely covering how generative models can propose biological designs and what that means for science, safety, and ethics.

Related MIT Technology Review coverage urges caution about AI hype, noting that LLMs still do not reason like AlphaGo, recursive self-improvement may be slow, and AI agents are not yet creative enough for open-ended research.
The work raises dual-use questions: AI-designed viruses could advance medicine and vaccines, but also pose biosecurity risks if not governed by strong synthesis screening and oversight.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals biology as a major frontier for generative models, expanding AI's role from software into engineered living systems. Developers may need new safety evaluations, DNA synthesis screening, and dual-use governance before releasing biological design tools. For regular users, the long-term payoff could include better vaccines, gene therapies, and diagnostics, but the same methods could lower barriers to dangerous biological design. The roundtable highlights a growing tension: AI can accelerate beneficial biology while forcing researchers, companies, and governments to build safeguards in parallel. Expect more scrutiny of model access, sequence screening, and responsible disclosure in coming years.
report.tools: To follow this space responsibly, watch genomic foundation models like Evo from the Arc Institute, protein-design tools such as RFdiffusion and AlphaFold/ESMFold, and protein language models including ESM. On the safety side, explore SecureDNA, IBBIS, and the Common Mechanism for DNA synthesis screening. These tools and frameworks show both the promise and the governance needs of AI-driven biology. None should be used to create harmful viruses; focus on published safety, biosecurity, and ethics resources.
